HORRIBLE OUTRAGE.
LEAVENWORTH, Kas., Sept. 25.—Near Grayson, a small town in Missouri, near this city, a terrible outrage was committed last night upon the person of Mrs. Winn, a young married woman, by an unknown man. Mrs. Winn lives a mile and a half from Grayson, and had been there to do some trading. When she returned home, at her gate, on alighting from her horse, an unknown man jumped from behind some bushes where he had been hiding, seized her, and accomplished his purpose after the poor victim had been exhausted by the most desperate struggle to prevent the terrible deed. The scoundrel died, and Mrs. Winn some time after remounted her horse, rode to Grayson, and told her sad story. In half an hour seventy men were in the saddle and united in searching the country for the villain, but at last accounts he had not been captured. Suspicion attaches itself to a stranger who had been loading around Grayson several days, and there is such strong feeling that if this man is captured the most trivial circumstances against him will undoubtedly cause him to be lynched, as but a short time ago at Platte City, near Grayson, a negro confined in jail for raping a white woman was taken from jail and hanged.

From the Liberty Advance of a couple of week or more ago, we take the following:

Among the most pleasant and enjoyable club meetings in Liberty are those of the "Larks" a musical association composed of both ladies and gentlemen. On Tuesday evening the "Larks" met at the Arthur House, and Judge Dunn was the special guest of the evening. By request he favored the Society with some selections on his favorite instrument—the violin. Judge Dunn was presented with a boquet of rare and beautiful flowers, in behalf of the ladies of the Society, by Wm. M. Barris, Jr., accompanied by a few very appropriate remarks, indicating that while the sterner sex recognized in him and accorded to him the high honor of being an upright man, an able lawyer and an honest Judge, the ladies wished to show their appreciation of his cultivation of the finer arts, music and poetry. In reply Judge Dunn expressed himself as overpowered by the kindness and good feelings toward him as expressed by the presentation of the boquet and accompanying remarks. It carried him back to the days when his heart, too, was young—the boquet should be taken to the one whom he had won as the bride of his youth and was now the wife of his maturer years, and by her cherished on account of the good feeling of the ladies of Liberty towards her husband. He congratulated the young men on their exalted privilege of being thrown in the society of ladies who by the rearing of such flowers showed marks of refinement and culture. Among those present on the occasion were Missis Flora Dougherty, Annie Park, Emma Reed, Katie Reed, Sallie Rouse, Dora Miller, Susie Allen, Annie Hale, Mrs. Alice Rohman, G. W. Corbin and wife, J. R. Timberlake and wife, W. M. Burris and wife, and Messrs. B. B. Corbin, Frank Corbin, J. M. Corbin, Jno. D. Thompson, R. G. Newlee, E. D. Miller, John Dougherty, Madison Miller, Eugene Chapman and Mr. Phelps. During the evening Miss Susie Allen gave the Society a recitation which was highly appreciated. Altogether the evening's entertainment was most happy, and the editor of the Advance, to whom an invitation was kindly extended, sorrowfully regrets his inability to be present.

The Missour City correspondent of the Liberty Tribune, says: A gentleman by the name of Bray, living near Vibbard, Ray county, while on his way to the Kansas City Fair, and when near this city, received an accidental shot in the fleshy part of the hip, by the discharge of a pocket pistol carried in his hip pocket. Dr. Posey dressed the wound, and he returned home this evening, not well satisfied with his part in the Fair.

A Republican paper says that the party in Maine is "like Lazarus—licked by dogs." We believe the sacred record explains the provocation of the canine attention referred to.

Colorado will have an election next Tuesday, for State officers, and Congressmen. It has been in the habit of going Republican, and voted for Hayes in 1876, but as the tide is turned now in favor of the Democracy, we may reasonably expect a Democratic victory. The elections in Ohio and Indiana take place one week from next Tuesday.

A negro committed a rape upon the person of Mrs. Benjamin Winn, a married lady, in Clinton county, last Saturday, and was hung by a mob that night. This was short work, but lustful brutes must understand that punishment will be short and swift for such offences. It is the only way to stop it.

Gen. Doniphan has written a letter from New York, to Dr. H. C. Garner, in which he gives a vivid account of the recent monster Democratic meeting in that city. He says there were 30,000 men in uniform, bearing torches in the procession, and not less than 125,000 people attended the meeting. There was speaking from 30 different stands, and all were crowded. It was, no doubt, the largest political demonstration ever made on the American Continent. The Democracy of New York are thoroughly united, and Hancock's majority will necessarily be very large. Gen. Doniphan also attended a meeting of Hancock Republicans, presided over by Leonard W. Jerome, while in New York, and he was much pleased with their proceedings.

Lexington Intelligencer: Our wheat men are paying from 76 to 80 cents. * * * The butchers are pleased with the cool night. * * * Work is soon to be commenced on the river improvement at this place. * * * Albert Fischer, son of Jno. G. Fischer, fell out of a walnut tree a few days ago, and broke both bones of the right wrist. Under Dr. Atkinson's skillful care he is doing well. * * * Mr. J. J. Browning, who has been running a threshing machine the past season, has threshed over 24,000 bushels of wheat, and has about 12,000 bushels more to thresh.

Elder J. J. Errett, a well known minister of the Christian Church, died recently, sitting in his chair, at his home in Pike county. At the time his wife was absent on a visit to a neighbor, when a small colored boy happened to pass Mr. Errett's residence, saw him fall to the floor, and immediately hastened for a physician, but when the doctor came Mr. Errett was lying on the floor dead. We knew him in our boyhood days, and a better or more popular minister did not live in the eastern part of the State. He was aged about sixty-five years, and many warm friends will mourn his sudden death.—Carrollton Democrat.

There is a Baptist minister in Kentucky who doesn't believe in missionary effort. He interprets the Bible to say that when the Gospel is preached to all the people the end of the world will come, and he will not contribute a cent or lift a finger to hasten that awful period.

Max Adler's old story of the fellow that serenaded his girl for two solid hours before he discovered that her folks had moved out, and the house was placarded "to let," was realized down at Vineland the other night, and the enterprising real estate agent for the house in question utilized the event to get a good free advertisement out of the local newspaper.

The Cleveland Press says: The valuable trunk that was stolen from Miss Smith, of Oberlin college, at the beginning of the term, has been found in the woods near the city, robbed of its contents and $200 in money. The thief got more ruffles, furbelows and garments, decorated with embroidery in the highest style of delirium tremems art, than he can wear out in a century.

A woman was murderously assailed in Clinton county, Kansas, and a lynching party was soon formed to hunt the villain. Henry Bird joined the mob and was foremost in the search. At length a scratch on his neck drew attention, and other evidence convinced his companions that he was the man whom they sought.—They hanged him promptly.

John Moran was under engagement to Lottie Church, at Sandy Lane, Ala.—He deserted her and went to live in an adjoining county. When told of his perfidy, she prayed that he might be punished by instant death. It chanced at exactly that hour he was killed by the fall of a tree.
I beg your pardon, sir," said one of the three men who entered Dovey's store at Mercer's Station, Ky., "but will you please hand me five hundred dollars out of your safe?" and he politely leveled a revolver. "Sorry to disoblige," Dovey replied, "but there isn't a cent there;" and he affably opened the safe for them to see. The robbers made a thorough search and then withdrew.

At the sale of a herd, of a noble stock owner, in England, the other day, two young bull calves of the purest bred short-horned family to be found in Britain, with a pedigree back to the fifteenth generation, were sold to the owner of a Californian ranch for 800 guineas apiece. The owner had his costly purchases conveyed to town in a special wagon, and then had their lives insured at a high premium before starting on their long westward journey.

JERSEY CITY, N. J., Sept. 27.—The work at the tunnel was resumed at six o'clock this morning with an extra force of men. They commenced cutting away the iron plates of the tunnel, which prevented the lowering of the caisson. By six o'clock this evening that was accomplished, and the caisson was lowered two feet, when eight bodies were discovered, and shortly afterward taken out of the caisson, and from there to the Morgue. Of the eight bodies taken out four were identified as the remains of Bryan Sheridan, James Creavey, Thomas Burns and Michael Bröderick. It was impossible to recognize the others.

A Washington dispatch of the 27th says: The second auditor of the treasury has written to Secretary Sherman on the subject of the safe robbery. He says: In reply to your oral inquiry of this morning, I have the honor to report that in December last it was discovered that $4,740 in money and bonds, including interest, were missing from the safe of this office. Thorough investigation established the fact that the funds had been abstracted by Chas. F. Herring, deputy auditor, who died November 29, 1879. There is no evidence that a single dollar of the missing funds belonged to deceased soldiers. On the contrary the bulk of it consisted of bonds taken from soldiers at draft rendezvous in 1864 and 1865, assured against their desertion. It is also said that as neither the money nor bonds had been called for, the soldiers from whom they were taken became bounty jumpers.

The discovery has been made at Washington that the effects of deceased soldiers in the custody of the second auditor of the treasury have been stolen. These valuables, which consisted of watches, chains, pocket-books, bonds, and miscellaneous trinkets were picked up by nurses, surgeons, and others, on various battle-fields during the war for the Union, and many of them are marred by bullets or stained by the blood of the owners. They were kept in a safe in Auditor French's office, to which several clerks had access. French and Herring, his assistant, are dead, and it is suspected that with them is buried the secret of the manner in which the property was stolen, as it is now known that it dssappeared some years ago.

Formal charges have at last been filed against Fitzsimmons, United States marshal of Georgia. They were prepared by a special agent of the treasury department who was sent South to investigate the alleged shortcomings of this official, and who finds them about as reported by his enemies. Among other things he is said to have obstructed the execution of federal laws within his jurisdiction, and to have swindled the government and oppressed the people in many ways.

A table compiled by the commissioner of internal revenue shows that laborers in the temperance vineyard are not making much headway. A little orphan girl, living in the family of Mr. and Mrs. Andrew Crawford, near Belvidere, Ill., was whipped regularly three times a day until she grew tired of it, and took to the woods. She was found by a sympathizing person, to whom she told her sad story, and who immediately placed Mrs. Crawford under arrest.

A Washington dispatch of the 1st says: The daughter of ex-president Zachary Taylor was paid $16,000 to-day, the balance of the salary which Gen. Taylor would have received had he lived till his term of office expired.

The National Fair association will hold its fair in Washington, next month, and offers $25,000 in premiums. St. Julien will be there, but it is feared that President Hayes will miss the show.

The Sixteenth infantry, now serving in Kansas, with headquarters at Fort Riley, has been ordered to exchange stations with the Twenty-fourth infantry, headquarters at Fort Davis, Texas.

A Leavenworth dispatch of the 28th says: The people of Leavenworth were shocked this morning by the report of another murder, which, according to the statement of half a dozen eye witnesses, was one of the most cold blooded crimes ever committed in the county. The murder was committed by James Kilker, a former policeman of the city, in a saloon kept by himself, and the victim was Samuel Byrns, a younger brother of Clark Byrns, the liveryman. The particulars of the bloody affair are substantially as follows: About two years ago Kilker and Byrns had a personal altercation, which resulted in Kilker having his arm broken. Since that time the parties have not spoken, though there has been no other quarrel between them. At an early hour yesterday morning—about 2 o'clock—Byrns was going home, when he met a party of friends, and one of the company proposed to have a drink. This he declined, but said he would take a cigar. Kilker's saloon on Fifth street, near the police alley, being the most convenient, the company went in and walked up to the bar, but before they had time to give their orders. Kilker drew from beneath the counter a navy revolver, and, leveling it at Byrns, fired without speaking a word. The shot took effect in the young man's abdomen, passing through his body, and severed his spinal column, resulting in death in a few moments. Deputy Marshal Doveran, having observed Byrns enter the saloon, and being aware of the old difficulty between the two men, followed him into the saloon, and was present at the shooting. Kilker, with the pistol still in his hand, was immediately arrested by Doveran, and locked up in the city prison. Byrns was a mere boy, not yet twenty years old, and, though a little wild at times, was a good hearted fellow, and not regarded as a bad man. He had been married less than a year before, and has a child only a few weeks old. At the time of the shooting his wife was absent from the city, visiting friends, and has been summoned home by telegraph to attend the funeral of her husband. HANGED.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

SHELBY, N. C., Dec. 17.—Daniel Keith, a white man, was hung in Rutherfordton today in the presence of an immense crowd, estimated at 7,000. He got up this morning early and ate a hearty breakfast, after carefully washing himself. He was taken from his cell at 11 a.m. to the gallows, a distance of half a mile. He rode in an open wagon, the great crowd following him. It was more like a plenile than a hanging occasion, and the crowd, as it jostled after the poor devil, seemed to be in the best humor. His coffin, which, by his own request, had been in his cell three days with him, was put in the wagon and used as a seat.

When the motley procession reached its destination, Keith was helped out. He requested permission to look into his grave, which had been dug in the field about twenty feet from the scaffold. This was granted, and he looked into the yawning pit calmly, and then with a firm step ascended the scaffold. His spiritual comforter, the Rev. Mr. Osborn, then offered a prayer, after which the doomed man spoke as follows:

"LADIES AND GENTLEMEN: You see now what whisky has done for me. I want all you young people to take warning from my fate. You know the devil sets up his shops about a mile from your towns, and then the trouble begins. I wish there was not a drop of whisky in the world."

Some one here asked him if he was ready to die. He replied:

"I hope I am. I have done all I could, and trust to God for the rest. Let my sad death be a fair warning to all whisky-drinkers and sinners. My own meanness brought me to the gallows. I trust I have truly repented. A year ago I was a free man, running around drinking and fiddling, without fear of God even. To-day I am on the gallows. Judgment will come to all down in this large crowd I see before me. Judgment will come when you do not look for it."

In closing he asked his friends to see that his body was not interfered with, and said:

"I thank God that I am willing to give my life for that I took. I never took that of any other person." He spoke slowly and in a firm voice, and then knelt and prayed, after which he gave some directions to his friends about his private affairs. He shuddered when the rope was put over his neck, and said, "It's cold, ain't it?" He took the handkerchief from the Sheriff, and after the black cap had been placed over his head he dropped the handkerchief, and at this signal he swung into the unknown. Time, 12 o'clock. His neck was broken and his struggles were slight.

THE CRIME.

Keith murdered Alice Ellis, a colored girl aged 13 years, after attempting to commit an outrage upon her person. He moved to Cleveland County about December, 1879, and rented a farm on which there were two small houses, in one of which he lived, while the other was occupied by Thornton Ellis with his wife and daughter, the latter being Keith's victim. On the day of the murder, Keith went to a neighbor's house, about a mile distant from his own, and told a long story of his having been assaulted by an escaped negro convict, for whose apprehension a large sum of money had been offered. Keith proposed that they should go in search of the convict and divide the reward. The neighbor, while doubting somewhat the statement made by Keith, started out with him, but had not gone far before he began to suspect Keith of lying, and turned back. Keith, however, got several other neighbors to go with him, after telling them the story of

THE PRETENDED ASSAULT and the large reward. His aim was to lead them to the spot where his victim had been murdered, and he expected them to draw the conclusion that the convict of whom he had spoken had committed the murder. He carried the party to a wild place in the woods, where the body of the girl lay; and he pretended to discover it. The girl was unconscious. By her side there was a large stone covered with blood, and the ground indicated that she had made a desperate struggle for her life. She died in a few hours after she was discovered. The physician who examined her body said that a rape had been attempted, but had not been accomplished owing to her age, she being only 13 years old.

Suspicion at once attached to Keith, who was confused in his statements, and finally he was arrested. Owing to the feeling against him, the case was removed to Rutherfordton, where he picked out a jury of white men. He was

FOUND GUILTY OF MURDER

In the first degree, and sentenced to be hanged. His counsel took an appeal to the Supreme Court, but that court affirmed the decision of the lower court, and Keith was sentenced to be hanged on the 17th of December. He received the sentence in a very indifferent manner, and went back to his cell as unconcerned as when he first entered it. A short time before his execution he made a full confession of his crime. It seems that he had followed the girl into the field, and then enticed her into the woods, where he made his hellish attempt upon her. She made a desperate resistance; but he finally succeeded in overpowering her. Fearing her screams would be heard, he picked up a large rock and crushed in her skull.

Keith was born in Kentucky. He was a man of powerful physique, being six feet in height, and weighing 200 pounds.

A KENTUCKY MANGING.
A Kurderer Swings off After a Private Fashion.
CINCINNATI, February 24.—John Major Hiecks, a colored man, born in Boyd county, Ky., April 15, 1862, was hanged at Covington to-day. The execution was the second one ever had in Kenton county, and was the first quasi private execution in the State of Kentucky, and is likely to be the last, as the law requiring executions in an inclosure has just been repealed and will go into effect in thirty days. This execution was held in a shell of a building, built of brick. All of the outside lower story windows were nailed up with boards. The condemned man was brought on the scaffold, attended by Father McGinley, Father Lambert and two other priests. At seven minutes past ten o'clock they knelt and prayed audibly, the prisoner repeating after Father McGinley the Lord's Prayer and the Apostle Creed. After this the prisoner was brought to the platform, where he shook hands with the priests. Then Father Lambert came to the front, and addressing the three hundred spectators admitted, said: "Mr. Hiecks will say nothing; I speak for him. He takes this death as a punishment for his sins."

The noose was then fixed, his hands manacled and the strips of the black cap were adjusted, Hiecks all the while weeping profusely, and exclaiming: "God is good! Oh! Lord Jesus, have mercy!" The priests exhorted him with the words: "Trust in Jesus. He can save the soul." The trap dropped at 10:15, and the body was cut down at 10:44. There was no struggling. He was hung for the murder of Henry M. Williams, at Ludlow, Ky., December 15th, 1880, early in the evening. There were no living witnesses to the crime. This utterance of Father Lambert on the scaffold is the only confession he made.

SOUTH CAROLINA METHODS.
"Visitors" at Work in Newberry-Black Sheep Try to Bite White Wolves in Edgefield-One Sheep Killed and Thirteen Wounded-No Wolves Hurt.
A dispatch from Newberry county, S. C., printed in the Columbia Register says:

The election has passed off quietly and without any disturbance save in the upper part of the county, where forty mounted men from parts unknown swooped down like an avalanche upon the voters, white and colored, who were around the ballot-box, precipitating a row and eventually resulted in the killing of one colored man. The sheriff was notified and repaired with a posse of fifty men to the scene of the difficulty, and from last accounts peace had been restored. It was an unprovoked attack, which has called forth the condemnation of both parties. The visitors were not of Newberry.

At Johnston's, in South Carolina, a riot occurred between the whites and the blacks. The latter tried to seize the ballot-box. One negro was killed and thirteen wounded. A telegram has been received here from Aiken, S. C., stating that the negroes have threatened to burn that town tonight, and asking for assistance. The election was very quiet. There was no disturbance whatever. The negro vote is the largest in ten years, and they voted the republican ticket almost solidly.
warren-williams-1880-11-02.A2:
THE ELECTION!
A COMPLETE TRIUMPH!
WHITE AND BLACK VOTING TOGETHER!
The election Tuesday, 2nd, passed off quietly, with one exception. The tickets in the field were (1) the straight Democratic ticket, and (2) a Republican Presidential and Congressional ticket, and the following persons for County officers: For the Senate, Ellison S. Keitt; for the House of Representatives, Jno. C. Wilson, Jas. A. Crotwell and David B. Lyles. Mr. Wilson was a regular nominee on the Democratic ticket. The Clerk, Sheriff, Probate Judge and School Commissioner on this ticket were the regular Democratic nominees. The County Commissioners on this ticket were, J. D. S. Livingston, Sam'l W. Cannon and Lewis Duckett, col.

By whom this latter ticket was gotten up we do not know. Mr. Livingston knew nothing of it till the morning of the election. Neither did Mr. Crotwell. The names of the other Democrats on the ticket were very probably used without their knowledge or consent; but this we do not know.

There was also a third ticket containing the Republican Presidential Electors, the Republican candidate for Congress, and the balance the regular Democratic nominees, State and County.

The colored people were very much
at sea, and their feelings were expressed by one who said that he was a Republican and wanted to vote a Republican ticket, but couldn't find one, and therefore he would as lief vote one of the tickets as the other. The Democrats worked hard all day, and whites and blacks voted together very generally. At all the boxes good order prevailed and only one incident happened to mar the harmony of the day. While the whites and blacks were voting quietly and peaceably at Cromer's Store a party of twenty-five or thirty young men, said to be from Laurens County, charged in on horses without any warning and attacked the negroes with clubs and pistols. One negro was killed. The whites at the polls banded together and protected the negroes from further harm. The negroes speak in the highest terms of the conduct of the Newberry whites, who came promptly to their rescue. Great indignation is felt by the whites as well as blacks of that community over the occurrence, and efforts will be made to bring the guilty parties to justice. The negro who was killed, Warren Williams, was a good negro. With this exception the day passed off pleasantly, and, as will be seen by the returns, the regular Democratic ticket received a large majority. Our report of the vote is not claimed to be correct; but is as nearly so as we can get it at this time. The vote for Electors and for Congressmen is very nearly correct; but the other is principally by estimate on the basis of the electoral vote. The Newberry box is accurate; in the others there are some mistakes—the general result, however, is about correct. The State goes Democratic by a large majority—25 or 30,000.

MURDER IN NEWBERRY.—To the Editor of the News and Courier: A party of unknown men rode up to the polls at Cromer's Precinct, and in a disturbance, which they raised, one negro was killed. The white people at the polls from the neighborhood did all they could to quiet the disturbance and finally succeeded in driving off the rioters. The affair is very much deplored by the whites, and the colored people entirely exonerate the citizens of Newberry County from any knowledge of the affair. A posse, headed by Sheriff Wheeler, is now on the grounds to keep down any further disturbance. An investigation of the matter is being had, and the guilty parties, if found out, will be punished. M. A. CARLISE, County Chairman.

ELECTION IN THE SOLID SOUTH.

It is quite probable that many people have never placed implicit confidence in the reports of Southern building, and have often believed them to be manufactured for political capital. We know of good Northern Republicans even who have had doubts as to the truthfulness of them. But the "doubting Thomases" must acknowledge after reading certain extracts from Democratic papers that the evidence leans strongly to the position that no more than the truth has been told of the horrible atrocities occurring from time to time in the South, which have been made public in the North. A gentleman now resides in this city who was once a prominent Republican in the South, and who can verify a greater part of the reports concerning the oppression of Republicans both white and black in the land of "red shirts," "ku klux," and "White Liners." State Senator Taft, writing to the Charleston (S. C.) News, gives a description of his treatment at a Republican meeting held at the county seat of Fairfield county. Here are some of his statements:

* * * I had not gone far before the Red-shirts, all of whom were mounted, and Democrats on foot, came rushing after me, with all sorts of epithets of the most obscene and profane character. Presently a hundred or more of the mounted men charged in my rear upon the colored men and myself, the street and opposite sidewalks being entirely filled with the Red-shirts on horseback.
